subject: literature
passage: Many picture books for young children repeat the same line again and again, such as a refrain that returns on every page. Literary scholar Fatima Zahra Benali argues that authors use these refrains to invite children to take part in the story. In her view, a repeated line lets children guess what comes next and say it along with the adult who is reading.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Benali's argument?

choices.A: Children usually listened quietly and rarely spoke when adults read books with refrains aloud.
choices.B: Picture books with refrains are often shorter than other picture books written for the same age group.
choices.C: Many authors of picture books draw the illustrations for their own stories.
choices.D: When adults read books with refrains aloud, children often said the refrain before the adult did.

explanation.why: Benali argues that refrains let children predict the next line and join in. Evidence that children actually say the refrain, even before the reader gets to it, supports her argument directly.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Children staying silent would suggest refrains do not get them to join in, which weakens the argument.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The length of the books says nothing about whether refrains invite children to take part.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Who draws the pictures has nothing to do with how refrains affect young listeners.
explanation.D: Correct. Children saying the refrain ahead of the reader shows that they predicted it and joined in, as Benali claims.
